gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured chamber temperature. Thomas Sanladerer (Toms3D) measured about 50 °C inside a Prusa CORE One during an ABS print, against about 40 °C maximum in a Bambu Lab X1 Carbon, which also has a passive enclosure like the P2S. 3DPrint.com measured the CORE One's ASA calibration parts within 0.05 mm on 100 mm.
standout_why: I opened both pages ChatGPT cited. goodprints3d.com gives no measured figures at all and says only that the CORE One has 'active temperature control', with no number. 3dprinterlab.net gives Bambu's 65 °C spec for the X2D and calls the P1S enclosure 'not heated'. It has no measurements. Of the top uncited results, speakcad.com/blog/best-3d-printer-for-functional-parts lists the CORE One as 'passive to about 55 °C', which is a spec with no tester named. It has no noise, accuracy or strength figures. None of the three pages names anyone who measured anything.
decides: For ABS, ASA or nylon parts, chamber heat is what separates ChatGPT's $449 P2S from the $1,149 CORE One+. Toms3D's side-by-side shows the CORE One's bed-heated, regulated chamber running about 10 °C warmer than a passive Bambu enclosure (about 50 °C vs about 40 °C), and the CORE One made the more accurate ABS part. This backs the CORE One+ for engineering materials, at the cost of about 30 minutes of preheat in a cool room. Two caveats: these tests used the original CORE One and the X1C, not the CORE One+ and P2S on the cards. For PLA and PETG parts the A1 and P2S stay the value picks. The QIDI Q2 that Dealectric lists has a 65 °C active chamber heater, and TechRadar's test puts its accuracy about level with the CORE One's (0.128 mm average X/Y error).

findings.note: This is the maker's own summary. The TechRadar original (https://www.techradar.com/pro/qidi-q2-3d-printer-review) would not load past its title, so the figures need checking against TechRadar before they go on the page. The 65 °C active chamber heating is QIDI's spec, not a measurement.
